Plaut. Curc. 516–516d: Heus tū, tibi ego dīcō.

Traupman 100: heus tū, tibi ego dīcō!
Traupman 410

tū, tuī

pronoun, second person: dative tibi, accusative and ablative tē; plural vōs · Wiktionary

you (one person)

As with ego, the verb’s ending says “you”, and tū is added only for stress or contrast: Quō nunc abīs? quīn tū hīc manēs? Latin says tū to anyone, a parent, a master or a stranger; there is no polite plural. “With you” is tēcum. Stronger, tūte (comedy) and tūte ipse.

Examples

  • Quō nunc abīs? quīn tū hīc manēs?

    Where are you off to now? Why don’t you stay here?Plaut. As. 597

  • numquid vīs? — Bene valē. — Valē. — Heus tū, tibi ego dīcō.

    Anything else? — Goodbye. — Goodbye. — Hey, you! I’m talking to you.Plaut. Curc. 516–516d

  • Salvum tē advenīre, Dēmea, gaudēmus. — Ehem, opportūnē: tē ipsum quaeritō.

    We’re glad to see you safely here, Demea. — Ah, just in time: you’re the very man I’m looking for.Ter. Ad. 80–81

  • Nōlī metuere: ūnā tēcum bona mala tolerābimus.

    Don’t be afraid: we’ll bear good and bad together with you.Ter. Ph. 556

  • difficilis facilis, jūcundus acerbus es īdem: nec tēcum possum vīvere, nec sine tē

    Hard and easy, sweet and sour, you are both at once: I can’t live with you, or without you.Mart. 12.46.1–2

  • Tūte hoc intrīstī: tibi omne est exedendum.

    You cooked this up yourself: you must eat it all up.Ter. Ph. 318

See also you, your, yourself, I.
